How the coins behave

A higher heads probability means that coin is more likely to produce H. The remaining probability belongs to tails.

F Fair coinHeads probability 50%
Allowed: 5–95%. A fair coin usually starts at 50%.
B Biased coinHeads probability 85%
Allowed: 5–95%. Higher means heads appears more often.
Dealer’s switching habits Advanced
Allowed: 5–95%. Higher means fewer switches away from Fair. Allowed: 5–95%. Higher means fewer switches away from Biased.

The dealer starts with an equal chance of holding either coin. Switching is the remaining probability.

04 · Plain-language guide

What does everything on the screen mean?

The app is a safe place to experiment. Change one setting, decode again, and notice how the hidden route responds. There is no score to win.

What you control

Inputs: evidence and assumptions

Observed tosses
The H and T results you heard. These are the visible evidence.
Heads probability
How often each coin is expected to land heads. Tails receives whatever probability remains. For example, 85% heads means 15% tails.
Keep the coin
How likely the dealer is to reuse the same coin on the next toss. A high value encourages longer runs with fewer switches.

What the model returns

Outputs: the model’s explanation

Hidden route
Viterbi’s single best Fair/Biased path for the complete sequence.
Path probability
The probability of that exact hidden route together with all the observed tosses. Small values are normal, especially for long sequences.
Fair / Biased bars
The probability of each coin at the selected step after considering the whole sequence. The two bars always total 100%.
The rule to remember

HMM results depend on the assumptions you enter. If you change how biased the coins are or how often the dealer switches, the best route may change. That sensitivity is part of the lesson—not a mistake in the app.

Things to notice while you play
  • A run of heads usually supports the biased coin.
  • Tails usually supports the fair coin under the starting values.
  • Higher “keep” values make the model resist frequent switching.
  • Similar coins make the tosses less informative.

Based on the hidden two-coin experiment in L. R. Rabiner’s HMM tutorial.
